title: Post-hoc Probabilistic Vision-Language Models
one_liner: Bolt uncertainty bands onto pre-trained image-text models without retraining by measuring how confident the final projection layers are.
lead: Pre-trained image-text models like CLIP map images and text to shared spaces, but they give single deterministic answers with no sense of confidence. When the model encounters data from a different domain or a tricky example, it commits to a guess without admitting uncertainty. This paper adds a confidence layer on top of the frozen model by asking: how much wiggle room is there in the final projection layers (the small networks that reshape the outputs before similarity scoring) if we tried to retrain them? The answer is a pair of numbers for each image-text pair: a point estimate and a confidence band around it.

paras: A standard vision-language model like CLIP takes an image and a text description, encodes each separately, then measures how similar they are via a single cosine similarity score. That score determines if they match. But the score is just a number with no tag that says how confident the model is.

A beginner might try fine-tuning the model on new data to learn when it should be uncertain, but that wastes the pre-training and demands retraining from scratch every time. A safer beginner idea is adding a separate neural net on top to predict uncertainty, but that net also needs training, adding compute cost and slowing down when the model answers new questions.
The real bind: pre-trained models are locked (frozen); adding uncertainty without training new numbers seems impossible.

callout.html: Estimate uncertainty by mathematically asking how the final projection layers would shift if lightly retrained, without actually retraining them.

panels.title: 1. Normal inference
panels.caption: Pre-trained model outputs one confidence number per image-text pair.

panels.title: 2. Projection layers act like gates
panels.viz_args: Image output → Projection gate → Similarity score
panels.caption: Last layer (projection) reshapes the output before matching against text.

panels.title: 3. Measure the local curvature
panels.caption: Hot regions resist change strongly; free regions shift easily under retraining.

panels.title: 4. Curvature becomes uncertainty
panels.viz_args: High curvature → Low uncertainty | Low curvature → High uncertainty
panels.caption: Steep terrain means stable, confident predictions; flat terrain means wobbly.

panels.title: 5. Attach confidence bands
panels.caption: Each similarity score now carries a confidence interval, no retraining.

steps.text: Keep the pre-trained image and text encoders frozen; only the projection layers are movable.
Compute the Hessian (a matrix that says how steeply the loss rises in each direction) of the projection layers using the pre-training data or a proxy dataset.
Use the Laplace approximation (a mathematical recipe) to estimate what the range of plausible projection layer weights would be.
Transform the projection layer uncertainty into uncertainty over the cosine similarity scores between images and text.
For any new image-text pair, produce both a point similarity score and a confidence interval around it, when answering questions.

paras: The paper modifies only the projection layers—the small neural networks at the end of the image and text processing models that shape the outputs before similarity scoring. Everything upstream (the main image and text processing models) stays untouched. By placing a probabilistic model over the projection layers (instead of deterministic numbers), the paper converts single similarity scores into pairs of (mean score, confidence band).

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: how steeply the loss rises
hidden.name: Hessian of the projection layer loss
paras: The hidden quantity is the Hessian—a matrix that records how sharply the training loss rises or falls in every direction around the current projection layer weights. A high Hessian value means the loss is steep in that direction: if you nudge that weight, the loss shoots up. A low Hessian value means the loss is flat: nudges barely change anything.

The paper estimates this Hessian by scanning through the pre-training data and accumulating how the loss changes with respect to each projection weight. This curvature map is the foundation: high-curvature weights are confident (locked in by the training data); low-curvature weights are uncertain (the training data was indifferent to their exact values).

heat.caption: Darker means higher Hessian value, steeper loss rise, and lower uncertainty.

reads.html: The loss is like a valley floor; steep walls mean the weight is pinned down; flat floors mean it can wander.
The Laplace approximation assumes the weights form a bell-curve pattern (a probability shape) centered at the trained values, with width determined by the Hessian inverse.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: from curvature to confidence
paras: When a model's projection layers have high curvature (the loss rises steeply), the pre-training data has tightly constrained those weights: moving them slightly breaks the training loss. This means new examples that rely on those weights get stable, reproducible predictions. Conversely, flat regions indicate that many different weight settings worked equally well on the training data. For a new example, those uncertain weights can swing around without violating training loss, so the final similarity score becomes wobbly.

The Laplace approximation converts this intuition into math: it models the projection weights as a bell-curve pattern (a probability shape) of plausible values centered at the trained point, with width determined by the Hessian. Given this pattern over weights, the paper analytically computes a similar pattern over the cosine similarity scores (via a formula involving the weight pattern and the outputs). The result is a similarity score plus an uncertainty band, derived purely from how steep or flat the loss terrain is, without touching the model.

The mechanism is mechanical: steep terrain near good weights means stable, narrow predictions; flat terrain means wide, uncertain predictions. No new numbers to train, no retraining, just measuring the terrain.

stages.s: Pre-trained image-text model with frozen encoders
Compute Hessian of projection layers from pre-training data
Apply Laplace to find the range of plausible projection weights
Push weight uncertainty through to similarity score uncertainty
Similarity score with confidence interval at test time

math.h2: The equation: from weight uncertainty to score uncertainty
math.words: The similarity score is the cosine of the projected image embedding and projected text embedding. If the projection layer weights are uncertain (distributed as a Gaussian), then the score is also uncertain. The Laplace approximation gives the covariance of that score uncertainty.
math.equation: sim(x_img, x_txt) = cos(P(phi(x_img)) / ||P(phi(x_img))||, Q(psi(x_txt)) / ||Q(psi(x_txt))||); var[sim] ≈ g^T * H^{-1} * g where g is the gradient of sim w.r.t. weights, H is the Hessian
symbols: the cosine similarity between projected image and text embeddings
the projection layer weight matrices for image and text
the frozen pre-trained image and text encoders
the Hessian matrix (second derivatives of training loss)
the gradient of the similarity score w.r.t. projection weights
the variance (squared width) of uncertainty around the similarity score

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose an image-text pair has similarity score 0.85 with the frozen model.
The Hessian at the projection layers shows: dimension 1 has value 100 (steep), dimension 2 has value 5 (flat).
The rate of change of similarity with respect to each dimension is rate_1 = 0.1, rate_2 = 0.2.
Uncertainty in dimension 1: (0.1) times (0.1) divided by 100 = 0.0001 (small, because steep terrain).
Uncertainty in dimension 2: (0.2) times (0.2) divided by 5 = 0.008 (larger, because flat terrain).
Final answer: similarity = 0.85 plus-or-minus 0.09, a confidence interval built from how steep or flat the loss terrain is.

math.note: Steep loss terrain makes the projection weights insensitive to nudges, so similarity predictions are tight; flat terrain makes weights swing freely, so similarity predictions are wide.

charts.title: Naive fine-tuning
charts.note: Fine-tuning for uncertainty loses efficiency and forces retraining for every new dataset.

charts.title: This paper (BayesVLM)
charts.note: Post-hoc Bayesian uncertainty adds negligible compute (barely any extra arithmetic per example) and improves confidence bands because it measures the steep or flat terrain instead of guessing, and never needs to retrain.

items.html: The Hessian computation must scan pre-training data (or a large proxy dataset), which may not be available for proprietary models. This breaks the pure post-hoc dream on closed models.

The Laplace approximation assumes the projection layer outputs follow a bell curve pattern (a probability shape). Real outputs may have outliers or skew, breaking the assumption and inflating or deflating uncertainty bands.

The uncertainty only accounts for the projection layer weights, not variations in the frozen encoders. Uncertainty in the encoder outputs themselves is ignored, potentially undercounting total uncertainty.
The math treats image and text projection layer uncertainties as independent, which is an approximation. In reality, the encoders may be coupled, violating this assumption.

When the data is in-distribution and the model is well-trained, the uncertainty bands are well-calibrated: scores that the model flags as uncertain are genuinely harder to predict, and confident scores are stable across domains.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small active learning loop: train a classifier on a small labeled subset of a vision-text dataset (e.g., a domain-shifted split of CIFAR or ImageNet captions), then use BayesVLM uncertainty to pick the next images to label. Compare against random selection or uncertainty from a naive fine-tuned model. The demo should show that BayesVLM picks harder, trickier examples (ones near decision boundaries or from rare regions), leading to faster accuracy growth per labeled example because the learner focuses effort on the toughest cases first.
demo.metric_eq: sample efficiency = number of labels needed to reach 90% accuracy; lower is better. Active learning gain = (random labels needed) / (BayesVLM labels needed) = should be > 1.5 for a meaningful result.
demo.closing: The demo must make impossible to miss that the model knows which examples it is uncertain about—and that certainty comes from measuring how steep or flat the loss terrain is, not from retraining.
